paragraphs.source_en: Today is Sunday, and the weather is splendid. My master came lumbering out of his study, arranged his brush, inkstone, and manuscript paper beside me, then lay on his stomach on the mat, steadily humming something under his breath. I suppose that, before beginning a draft, he first has to emit some odd sort of sound as a prelude. Watching closely, I saw that after a little while my master wrote, in thick dark ink and a heavy hand, the three large characters meaning ‘one stick of incense.’ How strange, I thought; could he be about to compose a poem or a haiku? For my master, a phrase like ‘one stick of incense’ seemed rather too refined and poetic. No sooner had I thought this than my master abandoned that line, started a fresh one, and wrote: ‘For some time I have wished to write about Tennen Koji.’ At that point his brush stopped, and would not move again. My master held the brush and tilted his head in thought. Apparently unable to come up with a good idea for how to continue, he began sucking the tip of the brush. When I looked, his lips had turned completely black. This time he drew a circle below, put two little dots inside it for eyes, added a flat little nose in the middle, and then drew one long horizontal line for a mouth. With that, it was no longer prose, nor was it haiku. My master himself seemed to feel that it was rather absurd, and hastily blacked out the face he had drawn. My master began another new line; apparently he vaguely believed that, so long as he changed lines, some poem, inscription, saying, or record would somehow emerge. Then, in a modern colloquial style, he dashed off a whole line at one stroke: ‘Tennen Koji was a man who studied space, read the Analects, ate roasted sweet potatoes, and let clear mucus drip from his nose.’ Well now! What a remarkably cluttered sentence that was. Then my master read it aloud without the slightest restraint and, quite unlike himself, laughed: ‘Ha ha ha... how amusing!’ Then he muttered to himself, ‘The bit about clear mucus dripping from his nose is a little too harsh; I’ll erase it.’ Saying this, he drew a vertical line through those words; one line would have been quite enough, but he drew two, then three, laying down neat parallel lines one after another, and even when they reached the neighboring line he paid no attention and kept going until there were eight lines in all, apparently still unable to think of how to continue. So he threw down the brush and took to twisting his moustache. He twisted it with such ferocity that he seemed to be declaring, ‘I shall twist an essay out of my moustache and show it to you.’ While he was twisting his moustache up and down, his wife came in from the living room, sat down plump in front of the tip of his nose, and said, ‘Listen, I have something to tell you.’ ‘What is it?’ My master was exceedingly cold; his voice sounded muffled, like a gong struck under water. His wife seemed dissatisfied with his reply and said again, ‘I said, I have something to tell you.’ My master said impatiently, ‘What is it, then?’ As he spoke, he thrust his thumb and forefinger into his nostril and sharply pulled out a nose hair.

paragraphs.source_zh: 今天是星期天，上好的天气。主人从书斋里慢条斯理地走出来，在我身旁摆上笔、砚和稿纸，然后趴在席铺上，嘴里不断哼着什么。大概是起稿之前先要发出一番怪里怪气的声音作为开端的吧。我留心看去，稍过一会儿，主人就用浓墨粗重地写上了“一炷香”三个大字。我想怪呀，莫不是要写诗或者俳句？对主人来说，所谓一炷香这种字眼，未免太蕴藉风流了吧。我刚想到这里，主人已不再理这一行，而重新改行，写道：“我早已欲写天然居士之事了。”他的笔写到这里停下来，再也不动了。主人拿着笔，歪着头在思考。看来，他想不出怎样往下写的好主意，便嘬起了笔尖。我一看，他的嘴唇全成黑的啦。这一次他在下边画了个圆圈，在圆圈中间点上了两个小点，算做眼睛，往正中间又画了个扁扁的鼻子头，然后又画上了长长的一横，算做嘴。这么一来，文章、俳句都做不成了。看来主人自己也感到不太像话，赶快又把画出的这张脸用墨涂掉。主人又开始改行写，看来他大概是漫无目的地认为只要改行，就会写出什么诗啦、赞啦、语录等等的吧。随后他用白话体一气呵成地写下了一行字：“天然居士是个研究空间、念《论语》、吃烤红薯、流清鼻涕的人，”好家伙！这个句子真够啰嗦的啦。然后主人毫无顾忌地朗读了起来，并且一反常态地大笑道：“哈哈……真有意思！”然后自言自语地说：“‘流清鼻涕’这句话也太损啦，抹去吧。”说着便在这四个字上划了一条竖线，本来一条线就足够了，可他却两条、三条，不断往上整整齐齐地划平行线，已经划到旁边的行上去，他也毫不在乎，照旧划下去，一共划了八条线，似乎还没想出如何往下写。于是他扔掉笔，拈起胡须来。他拼命地拈胡须，那势头就仿佛向人说：“我一定要从拈胡须中拈出文章来给你们看哩。”他正在把胡须拈上拈下，这当儿，主人的妻子从起居间走来，一屁股坐在主人的鼻子尖前，说道：“喂，我要跟你说件事儿。”“什么事儿？”主人十分冷淡，他的声音就好像在水里敲铜锣似的，闷声闷气。看来主人的妻子似乎不满意主人的答话，又说了句：“我说，我要跟你说件事儿。”主人不耐烦地说道：“什么事儿呀？”说着，把大拇指和食指捅到鼻孔里猛地拔下了一根鼻毛。
